en: Now, the other important differentiation we
have to make is where an agent runs,
on your machine or on a remote server.
Because that software that runs the agent,
which is also often called a harness, and
I'll get back to that term too,
can of course be installed on your machine.
You can download it onto your laptop and run
it there.
Again, you can download Claude Cowork and
use it on your machine to work on your files
that may be stored somewhere on your
machine.
Theoretically, it could also run on some
other server because if you're using ChatGPT
in the web, for example, that's clearly not
running on your machine. It's running on
some server by OpenAI. And still, this is
also an AI agent because it can also use
tools. It can perform web search, for
example. It can also read files, but only
files you upload. Very often, it's the
general agents that do run on your machine
because typically you want them to work with
files on your system. For example.
But they can also run on a server like
ChatGPT in the web or also like our customer
support agent.
This is an agent that's there for our entire
team, not just for me. Would be pretty bad
if it would be running on my system because
if I shut down my computer,
it would be offline. That's not great.
So we put that agent onto a remote server
and it runs there and we set it up such that
everybody from our team can simply tag it in
Slack and talk to it like this, and behind
the scenes, the request will then be sent to
the remote server and the agent will do its
work there.
This gives us one central place where the
agent runs and where all the information for
the agent lives and doesn't depend on the
machine of an individual employee, which is
of course very useful. So being aware of
these different environments where an agent
may run and when which environment makes
sense, as I just outlined, also is important
to know when talking about AI agents.
